subtopic_detail: Bleeding after intercourse in a woman whose most recent primary screening test for human papillomavirus was negative, with a fleshy growth visible at the cervical os
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman who has had spotting after intercourse on most occasions for the past four months, and occasionally a small amount of brown loss between periods. Her cycles are otherwise regular and not heavy.

She has had two vaginal births, uses condoms for contraception and has never smoked. Her cervical screening test 14 months ago was reported as human papillomavirus not detected. On speculum examination there is a smooth fleshy pedunculated lesion about 12 mm across protruding from the external os, and touching it with a swab reproduces a small amount of bleeding. The cervix is otherwise smooth, the vaginal walls look healthy and there is no abnormal discharge. Bimanual examination shows a normal sized mobile non-tender uterus with no adnexal mass.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated 12 mm lesion protruding from the external cervical os that bleeds on contact, remainder of the cervix smooth with no friability, healthy vaginal walls, uterus normal size mobile and non-tender, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test 14 months ago reported human papillomavirus not detected, urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Repeat the primary human papillomavirus screening test today
options.rationale: A repeat screening test in under five years does not address a visible cervical lesion, and a negative result would be falsely reassuring because screening is not designed to assess a mass that can be seen. Symptomatic visible lesions are investigated on their own merits regardless of screening status. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid and review her again in three months
options.rationale: An antifibrinolytic treats heavy menstrual bleeding from a normal uterine cavity and does nothing for contact bleeding from a discrete cervical lesion. Delaying assessment by three months leaves a visible lesion unexamined histologically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics and gynaecology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics and gynaecology

options.text: Remove the lesion and send it for histological examination
options.rationale: A symptomatic pedunculated cervical lesion is removed so that the postcoital bleeding is treated and the tissue can be examined, because although the great majority are benign polyps a small proportion harbour malignancy that no amount of screening will detect. Removal of a small pedunculated polyp can be performed in the clinic by avulsion with polyp forceps, with hysteroscopic removal reserved for a broad based lesion or one arising from the canal. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Take endocervical swabs and treat for pelvic inflammatory disease
options.rationale: Chlamydial cervicitis causes a friable inflamed cervix with discharge rather than a discrete pedunculated mass, and there is no discharge, pelvic tenderness or cervical excitation here. Swabs remain reasonable opportunistic practice but antibiotics do not treat the lesion causing her bleeding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling first
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is directed at intermenstrual and postmenopausal bleeding where the cavity is the suspected source, and it is not the priority when a bleeding lesion is directly visible on the cervix. Imaging is added if bleeding persists after the visible lesion has been removed. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

explanation.summary: Postcoital bleeding always requires the cervix to be seen, because the differential runs from benign polyps and ectropion through chlamydial cervicitis to invasive cervical cancer. Australia's primary human papillomavirus screening programme has high sensitivity for the precursors of squamous cancer, but it is a screening test for asymptomatic women and a negative result does not exclude a symptomatic lesion, partly because some adenocarcinomas and rarer histological types are less reliably detected. This is why the national guidance separates the screening pathway from the investigation of symptoms: any woman with persistent unexplained postcoital, intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding requires examination and, where a lesion is seen, histology, irrespective of her screening history. Cervical polyps are the commonest visible cause and removal is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: A negative screening test never excludes a symptomatic visible cervical lesion
Postcoital bleeding mandates direct visualisation of the cervix
Removal of a symptomatic polyp is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Small pedunculated polyps can be avulsed in clinic; broad based lesions need hysteroscopy
Persistent bleeding after polypectomy prompts endometrial assessment
explanation.pearls: Around 1 in 200 to 1 in 1000 clinically typical cervical polyps contains malignancy or premalignancy on histology, which is the entire reason the specimen goes to the laboratory rather than the bin after an otherwise routine clinic avulsion.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities
RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding
Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics and gynaecology
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

subtopic_detail: Antenatal serology at twelve weeks showing no protective antibody against rubella in a woman with no record of childhood immunisation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing the results of the first antenatal visit for a 27 year old woman at 12 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She arrived in Australia as a teenager and has no immunisation records from her country of birth.

She is well, has no rash and reports no recent contact with anyone unwell. Her booking bloods show rubella IgG below the protective threshold with rubella IgM not detected, and her varicella IgG is protective. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology are all negative, her blood group is O positive with no atypical antibodies, and her full blood count is within normal limits. She asks what should be done about the rubella result.

data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG below the protective threshold with rubella IgM not detected, varicella IgG protective, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative, human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, blood group O positive with antibody screen negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rubella status?

options.text: Reassure her, as the absent IgM excludes any risk to this pregnancy
options.rationale: A negative IgM shows she has no current infection but says nothing about her susceptibility, which is precisely what the low IgG demonstrates and what leaves her at risk for the remainder of this pregnancy and in future ones. Conflating absence of current infection with immunity is the reasoning error here. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.text: Give measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at her next antenatal visit
options.rationale: This is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy, so administering it antenatally is the specific error being tested even though the woman genuinely needs the vaccine. The indication is correct and only the timing is wrong. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy

options.text: Give rubella immunoglobulin now and repeat her serology in four weeks
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has a limited and contested role after a significant exposure in a non-immune pregnant woman and has no place in the absence of any exposure. It does not produce lasting protection and is not a substitute for vaccination. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy

options.text: Advise avoiding contact with unwell children and vaccinate after birth
options.rationale: The live vaccine must wait until after delivery, so the antenatal plan is counselling about avoiding contact with anyone with a febrile rash illness together with a clear arrangement to vaccinate postpartum before discharge, which is safe during breastfeeding. Documenting the plan at booking is what prevents the opportunity being missed, since non-immune women are commonly discharged unvaccinated. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the rubella IgG in the third trimester before making any plan
options.rationale: Antibody titres do not rise without exposure or vaccination, so repeating the test later in pregnancy will reproduce the same result and simply consumes the window in which the postpartum plan should have been made. Repeat serology is indicated after a documented exposure to assess for seroconversion. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

explanation.summary: Rubella serology is performed at antenatal booking not to diagnose infection but to identify susceptible women who can be protected before their next pregnancy, since congenital rubella syndrome causes deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects and intellectual disability with the greatest risk in the first trimester. The vaccine is live attenuated and therefore contraindicated in pregnancy, which creates the recurring clinical problem that the woman who most needs it cannot receive it at the moment her susceptibility is discovered. The reliable solution is to write the postpartum vaccination into the care plan at booking, because rubella containing vaccine is safe while breastfeeding and can be given before discharge from the maternity unit. Avoidance advice during the pregnancy is genuine but limited, and women should be told to present promptly if they develop a febrile rash illness or have contact with one, in which case paired serology is arranged.
key_points: Low rubella IgG identifies susceptibility, not current infection
Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy
Vaccinate postpartum before discharge; it is safe while breastfeeding
Titres do not rise without exposure, so repeat antenatal testing is futile
A febrile rash illness or contact in pregnancy warrants paired serology
explanation.pearls: Women should avoid pregnancy for 28 days after receiving a rubella containing vaccine, which is why the postpartum dose is given before discharge rather than deferred to a six week check when a new pregnancy may already be possible.

sources.label: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications
BMJ Best Practice: Rubella infection in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Choosing between maternal immunisation in late pregnancy and a monoclonal antibody for the newborn to protect an infant born in the middle of winter
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic in June seeing a 31 year old woman at 30 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first child was admitted at 7 weeks of age with bronchiolitis and needed two days of oxygen, and she wants to know what can be done to protect this baby.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal growth on her 28 week scan and a normal glucose tolerance test. She has already received her pertussis containing vaccine at 22 weeks and her influenza vaccine in April. She has no allergies and takes only pregnancy multivitamins. She plans a vaginal birth at term at her local hospital and intends to breastfeed.

data_table.Investigations: Growth scan at 28 weeks with estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile and normal liquor volume, oral glucose tolerance test within normal limits, pertussis containing vaccine given at 22 weeks, influenza vaccine given in April

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about protecting her baby from respiratory syncytial virus?

options.text: No protection is available until the infant reaches six months of age
options.rationale: Protection is available and is specifically directed at the first months of life, which is when the risk of severe disease is concentrated. Waiting until 6 months would leave the highest risk period entirely uncovered. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: Offer the maternal vaccine now, or the infant antibody after birth
options.rationale: Maternal vaccination is given in a defined window in late pregnancy so that transplacental antibody protects the infant through the first months, and where the mother is not vaccinated in that window or delivers too soon after it the alternative is a long acting monoclonal antibody given to the infant. At 30 weeks she sits within the maternal window and either route is appropriate, so the plan is to offer the vaccine now with the infant antibody as the fallback. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: Defer any decision until the baby shows signs of a respiratory illness
options.rationale: Both available strategies are preventive and must be in place before exposure, since neither treats established infection. Deciding at the point of illness forfeits the benefit entirely. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: Give the maternal vaccine immediately after the birth of the baby
options.rationale: Vaccinating after delivery leaves no time for transplacental antibody transfer, which is the entire mechanism by which maternal immunisation protects the newborn. Postpartum administration is the correct timing for a live vaccine such as rubella, not for this one. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: Rely on exclusive breastfeeding and avoiding contact with older children
options.rationale: Breastfeeding and reducing exposure are worthwhile general measures but they are substantially less effective than either specific strategy and are not an alternative to them. Offering them alone in place of available immunoprophylaxis understates what can be achieved. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Respiratory syncytial virus is the leading cause of infant hospitalisation in Australia and the burden is concentrated in the first six months of life, with the youngest infants at highest risk of apnoea and respiratory failure. Two complementary strategies now exist: a maternal vaccine given in a defined late pregnancy window so that antibody crosses the placenta, and a long acting monoclonal antibody given directly to the infant, which does not depend on maternal immunisation or on the interval to delivery. The two are alternatives rather than additions for most infants, and the practical decision turns on whether the mother received the vaccine at an appropriate gestation and how long before birth, with the infant antibody covering those born outside that window, born very preterm, or with conditions conferring extra risk. Programmes are seasonally aligned in most Australian jurisdictions because the virus circulates predominantly across the cooler months, so the timing of the expected birth relative to the season shapes the conversation.
key_points: Severe disease burden is concentrated in the first six months of life
Maternal vaccination in a late pregnancy window provides transplacental antibody
A long acting infant monoclonal antibody is the alternative route
The two strategies are alternatives for most infants, not additions
Seasonal alignment and the interval from vaccination to birth drive the choice
explanation.pearls: The interval between maternal vaccination and delivery is what determines whether the infant still needs the monoclonal antibody, because antibody transfer needs roughly two weeks, so a baby delivered within a fortnight of the maternal dose is managed as though the mother had not been vaccinated.

sources.label: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus
National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance: Respiratory syncytial virus immunisation programs
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: Burning nipple pain that lasts after every feed with shiny flaking skin on both areolae and white patches inside the baby's mouth
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman 5 weeks after a normal vaginal birth. She describes burning pain in both nipples that starts partway through each feed and continues for 20 to 30 minutes afterwards, radiating into the breast. It began about a week ago, having previously settled after the first fortnight.

A lactation consultant reviewed her attachment three days ago and documented a good latch with the baby's chin indenting the breast and no nipple distortion after the feed. On examination both nipples and areolae look shiny and slightly flaky with a pink hue, with no cracks, fissures or bleeding. There is no breast lump, no wedge shaped erythema and no tenderness on palpation of either breast. Her temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius. When you examine the baby you see white plaques on the inner cheeks and tongue that do not wipe away easily.

data_table.Examination: Both nipples and areolae shiny, pink and finely flaking without cracks or fissures, no nipple distortion after feeding, no breast lump or wedge shaped erythema, no breast tenderness, no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Infant oral examination showing adherent white plaques on the buccal mucosa and tongue that do not wipe away easily, infant weight gain tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start oral flucloxacillin and arrange breast ultrasound this week
options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal treatment and imaging are directed at mastitis or an abscess, which present with a tender wedge of erythema, a fluctuant lump or systemic upset, none of which is present here. Her temperature is normal and both breasts are soft and non-tender. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Refer for further attachment review and supply nipple shields
options.rationale: Poor attachment is the commonest cause of nipple pain overall, but it causes pain worst at the start of the feed with visible nipple distortion or trauma, and attachment has already been formally assessed as good. Repeating that assessment does not explain the areolar skin change or the infant's oral findings. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush

options.text: Advise expressing and cup feeding until the nipple pain has settled
options.rationale: Interrupting direct feeding risks supply and does not eradicate organisms colonising the nipple and infant mouth, so pain typically recurs on resumption. Temporary expressing has a role where nipple trauma is severe enough to prevent feeding, which is not the case here. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush

options.text: Refer her urgently for a punch biopsy of the affected areolar skin
options.rationale: Biopsy is directed at a unilateral persistent eczematous or ulcerated nipple change that fails to respond to treatment, where Paget disease of the nipple must be excluded. Bilateral symmetrical change with oral findings in the infant has a far more likely explanation that deserves a treatment trial first. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush

options.text: Treat mother and baby together and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Burning pain persisting after feeds with shiny flaking areolae in a woman with a documented good latch, alongside adherent oral plaques in the infant, indicates candidal infection of the nipple and infant mouth, and both must be treated simultaneously or reinfection continues between them. Breastfeeding continues throughout, with topical miconazole gel for the infant mouth and topical antifungal to the nipples after feeds. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush

explanation.summary: Nipple pain is among the commonest reasons Australian women stop breastfeeding earlier than they intended, and the differential is worth working through systematically rather than defaulting to a single cause. Poor attachment dominates the first fortnight and produces pain that is worst as the baby latches, with visible nipple compression or trauma. Pain that begins later, burns, persists after the feed and is accompanied by shiny flaking skin suggests candidal infection, which is confirmed clinically and supported by oral plaques in the infant; because organisms pass between mother and baby, treating only one of the pair leads to relapse. The other diagnoses to hold in mind are bacterial infection of a fissure, mastitis with its tender erythematous wedge and systemic features, nipple vasospasm producing blanching then pain in the cold, and the rare but important unilateral eczematous change of Paget disease of the nipple.
key_points: Early pain worst at latch suggests attachment; later burning pain after feeds suggests candida
Shiny flaking areolar skin with infant oral plaques supports the diagnosis clinically
Mother and infant must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection
Breastfeeding continues during treatment
Unilateral persistent eczematous nipple change needs biopsy for Paget disease
explanation.pearls: Nipple vasospasm is the mimic most often mistaken for candidal infection, and the discriminator is colour change in the cold with the nipple blanching white then turning blue or red before the burning begins, which points to warmth and management of Raynaud phenomenon rather than an antifungal.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain and thrush
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding problems

subtopic_detail: A perineal repair on day seven after birth with gaping edges, surrounding redness and offensive discharge but no collection on examination
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman in the day assessment unit on day 7 after a normal vaginal birth with a second degree perineal tear repaired with absorbable sutures. She reports increasing perineal pain since day 4, a smelly discharge and a sensation that the wound has come apart.

She is opening her bowels with the help of a stool softener and passing urine without difficulty. Her vital signs are pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air and temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius. On examination the perineal repair has partially separated over about 2 cm with the edges gaping, and the surrounding tissue is erythematous, indurated and tender with a thin offensive discharge. There is no fluctuant collection, no crepitus and no skin necrosis. Her uterus is well contracted at the level of the symphysis with no tenderness and her lochia is not offensive.

data_table.Examination: Partial separation of the perineal repair over approximately 2 cm with gaping edges, surrounding erythema induration and tenderness, thin offensive discharge, no fluctuant collection, no crepitus, no skin necrosis, uterus well contracted and non-tender with non-offensive lochia
data_table.Investigations: Wound swab taken for culture, full blood count showing white cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Remove all remaining sutures and arrange district nurse packing daily
options.rationale: Routine removal of all sutures and packing is not required and adds discomfort without improving healing when the wound is already partially open and draining freely. Suture removal is considered selectively where a retained suture is clearly acting as a focus of infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma

options.text: Reassure her that separation at this stage heals without specific treatment
options.rationale: Simple dehiscence without infection can indeed be managed conservatively, but the erythema, induration, fever and raised inflammatory markers here establish infection that requires antibiotics. Treating this as uncomplicated breakdown risks progression to a deeper pelvic infection or fistula. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma

options.text: Take her to theatre today for immediate resuturing of the perineum
options.rationale: Resuturing infected tissue leads to repeat breakdown, so secondary repair is deferred until the infection has been treated and the wound bed is clean and granulating, typically some weeks later. Immediate return to theatre is reserved for a large collection needing drainage or for suspected necrotising infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma

options.text: Start oral antibiotics with wound care and review in two to three days
options.rationale: A perineal wound infection with cellulitis but no collection or necrosis is managed with antibiotics covering skin and bowel flora, analgesia, hygiene and regular saline irrigation, allowing the wound to be left open to heal by secondary intention with early review to confirm improvement. Decisions about secondary repair are made once infection has resolved and the tissue has declared itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma

options.text: Arrange pelvic ultrasound and start intravenous antibiotics for endometritis
options.rationale: Endometritis presents with uterine tenderness, offensive lochia and often subinvolution, and here the uterus is well contracted and non-tender with normal lochia. The source of infection is clearly the perineal wound, which is what the examination localises. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Perineal wound infection and breakdown complicate a small but clinically important minority of vaginal births and are a major contributor to persistent postnatal pain, dyspareunia and dissatisfaction with care. The organisms involved reflect the site and include skin flora and bowel anaerobes, so empirical cover is broader than for a simple skin infection. The sequence that matters is to treat infection first and consider repair second, because suturing inflamed infected tissue reliably fails; wounds are cleaned, left open and allowed to granulate, and many heal acceptably without any further surgery. The features that change the tempo are a fluctuant collection needing drainage, extension into the ischiorectal fossa, involvement of an anal sphincter repair, and any suggestion of necrotising soft tissue infection with disproportionate pain, crepitus or rapidly advancing erythema, which is a surgical emergency.
key_points: Cover skin and bowel flora, since the site is colonised by both
Treat infection first; secondary repair follows once tissue is clean
Wounds are left open to granulate rather than immediately resutured
A fluctuant collection needs drainage rather than antibiotics alone
Disproportionate pain with crepitus suggests necrotising infection and urgent surgery
explanation.pearls: Where an obstetric anal sphincter injury repair is involved in the breakdown, the case is escalated to a colorectal or urogynaecology service rather than managed on the ward, because a failed sphincter repair carries a real risk of long term faecal incontinence and secondary repair technique differs.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of perineal trauma
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
BMJ Best Practice: Perineal wound complications

subtopic_detail: A dilated fluid filled tube on the left seen on scan before a first cycle of in vitro fertilisation in a woman with past chlamydial infection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman with three years of primary infertility who is about to begin her first cycle of in vitro fertilisation. She had chlamydial pelvic infection treated in her early twenties.

Her cycles are regular and her partner's semen analysis is within normal limits. Her anti-Mullerian hormone is appropriate for her age and her thyroid function is within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, a normal right adnexa, and a 4 cm elongated fluid filled sausage shaped structure in the left adnexa with incomplete internal septations, separate from a normal appearing left ovary. A hysterosalpingogram performed last month showed free spill of contrast on the right with a dilated non-filling left tube. She asks whether anything should be done before her transfer.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, uterus normal size and mobile on bimanual examination, mild fullness in the left adnexa without tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a normal uterine cavity, normal right adnexa, and a 4 cm elongated fluid filled structure with incomplete septations in the left adnexa separate from a normal left ovary; hysterosalpingogram with free right spill and a dilated non-filling left tube; anti-Mullerian hormone appropriate for age; thyroid function within normal limits; partner semen analysis within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before embryo transfer?

options.text: Remove the affected tube laparoscopically before proceeding to transfer
options.rationale: A dilated fluid filled tube reduces implantation and live birth rates after in vitro fertilisation and increases miscarriage, and removing it before transfer restores outcomes towards those of women without the abnormality. Salpingectomy is preferred to tubal occlusion where the anatomy permits, and it also removes a site of future ectopic implantation. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

options.text: Proceed with transfer and reassess the left adnexa afterwards
options.rationale: Proceeding without intervention accepts a measurably lower chance of live birth from a cycle that carries significant financial and emotional cost. Reassessing afterwards cannot recover an implantation opportunity that has already been lost. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

options.text: Aspirate the fluid transvaginally at the time of oocyte collection
options.rationale: Aspiration is an option where surgery is not feasible but the fluid reaccumulates, so the benefit is short lived compared with definitive removal. It is a compromise reserved for dense adhesions or a hostile pelvis rather than a first choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

options.text: Give a course of doxycycline and repeat her ultrasound in six weeks
options.rationale: Antibiotics treat active infection and do not reverse the established structural dilatation that follows previous tubal damage, so the scan appearance will be unchanged. A treatment course would be appropriate if there were current signs of pelvic inflammatory disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Attempt to reopen the distal end of the tube to restore its patency
options.rationale: Reconstructive tubal surgery has poor patency and pregnancy rates in a tube damaged enough to be dilated, and a reopened but non-functional tube leaves a significant ectopic risk. Its place is limited to selected younger women with minimal tubal damage who wish to avoid assisted reproduction. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

explanation.summary: Tubal factor infertility remains a major cause of subfertility in Australia and commonly follows chlamydial infection, which is frequently asymptomatic and therefore treated late or not at all. Where distal obstruction produces a dilated fluid filled tube, that fluid appears to reduce endometrial receptivity and may mechanically flush embryos, and randomised and pooled evidence shows that removing the tube before in vitro fertilisation improves implantation and live birth rates while reducing miscarriage. Salpingectomy is the preferred procedure because it is definitive, although proximal tubal occlusion is an accepted alternative where adhesions make the tube unsafe to remove, and transvaginal aspiration offers only temporary benefit. The counselling point for the woman is that the ovary and its blood supply are preserved during a properly performed salpingectomy, so ovarian reserve and her response to stimulation are not the trade off she may fear.
key_points: A dilated fluid filled tube lowers implantation and live birth rates
Removal before transfer restores outcomes towards baseline
Salpingectomy is preferred; proximal occlusion is the alternative for a hostile pelvis
Aspiration is temporary because fluid reaccumulates
Reconstructive surgery on a badly damaged tube leaves a significant ectopic risk
explanation.pearls: Women frequently decline salpingectomy fearing it will reduce their ovarian reserve, and the specific reassurance is that careful dissection close to the tube preserves the ovarian and infundibulopelvic vessels, with studies showing no meaningful fall in anti-Mullerian hormone or in the number of oocytes retrieved.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
Cochrane Review: Surgical treatment for tubal disease in women due to undergo in vitro fertilisation

subtopic_detail: A gestational sac sitting within the lower anterior uterine wall at the site of two previous operative scars with thin overlying myometrium
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment unit seeing a 36 year old woman at 7 weeks by dates with light vaginal bleeding for two days and mild suprapubic discomfort. She has had two previous caesarean sections and no vaginal births.

She is haemodynamically stable and her abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no guarding. Her serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin is 9400 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity and an empty cervical canal, with a gestational sac containing a 7 week foetal pole and cardiac activity embedded within the lower anterior myometrium at the site of the previous hysterotomy scars. The myometrium between the sac and the bladder measures 2 mm, and colour Doppler shows prominent peritrophoblastic flow around the sac. Both ovaries appear normal and there is no free fluid in the pelvis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no guarding, closed cervical os with a small amount of dark blood in the vault
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 9400 IU/L, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115 to 155), blood group A positive, transvaginal ultrasound showing an empty uterine cavity and empty cervical canal with a gestational sac containing a foetal pole and cardiac activity within the lower anterior myometrium at the previous scar site, myometrium between sac and bladder 2 mm, prominent peritrophoblastic Doppler flow, normal ovaries, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange suction curettage of the uterine cavity on the emergency list
options.rationale: Blind instrumentation of a pregnancy implanted within the scar risks perforation into the bladder and torrential haemorrhage, because the trophoblast has invaded myometrium rather than sitting in the cavity. Suction curettage is the correct procedure for an intrauterine miscarriage or a molar pregnancy, where the pregnancy lies within the cavity. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate and repeat levels weekly
options.rationale: Systemic methotrexate alone is a poor choice at this gonadotrophin level with demonstrable cardiac activity, and it has a high failure rate in scar implantation with a risk of delayed rupture during prolonged resolution. Methotrexate retains a role as an adjunct within a specialist protocol rather than as sole therapy here. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Refer to a specialist unit for planned treatment with theatre available
options.rationale: Implantation within a hysterotomy scar carries a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage and uterine rupture, so management is planned in a unit with interventional radiology and surgical support rather than improvised, using options such as ultrasound guided local injection, hysteroscopic or laparoscopic resection, with uterine artery embolisation available. Counselling covers the significant risk of hysterectomy and the recurrence risk in future pregnancies. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Observe with serial scans, as many of these pregnancies relocate upward
options.rationale: A pregnancy implanted in the scar does not migrate into the cavity, and expectant management is associated with rupture, massive haemorrhage and abnormally invasive placentation later in pregnancy. Serial observation is appropriate for a pregnancy of unknown location with low and falling gonadotrophin levels. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Perform laparoscopic salpingectomy on the side of the prominent flow
options.rationale: Removing a tube treats a tubal ectopic pregnancy, and both tubes and ovaries are normal here with the pregnancy clearly within the anterior myometrium. This distinction matters because the near pair is the far commoner tubal ectopic, which this scan specifically excludes. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

explanation.summary: Caesarean scar ectopic pregnancy is an increasingly encountered consequence of rising caesarean rates and is defined by implantation within the fibrous tissue of a previous hysterotomy scar, with an empty cavity and cervical canal and thinned myometrium between the sac and the bladder. It is dangerous in a way that a tubal ectopic is not, because the trophoblast invades a poorly vascularised scar adjacent to the bladder and to large uterine vessels, so both early rupture and later abnormally invasive placentation are real risks. There is no single established treatment and reported approaches include ultrasound guided intragestational injection, hysteroscopic or laparoscopic resection, and combined approaches with uterine artery embolisation, which is why the central decision for the receiving registrar is to move the woman to a unit resourced for these rather than to act locally. Documented recurrence in subsequent pregnancies makes early first trimester ultrasound in any future pregnancy part of the discharge plan.
key_points: Empty cavity and canal with a sac in the anterior scar defines the diagnosis
Thin myometrium between sac and bladder predicts rupture risk
Blind curettage risks perforation into the bladder and massive haemorrhage
Management is planned in a unit with embolisation and surgical support
Recurrence risk mandates early ultrasound in any future pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Residual myometrial thickness below about 3 mm between the sac and the bladder is the measurement that marks the highest risk group for rupture and heavy bleeding, and it is the number that pushes management towards resection with embolisation available rather than a medical approach alone.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Early pregnancy complications
BMJ Best Practice: Caesarean scar pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Bleeding years after the last period with a thickened endometrium and a solid ovarian mass whose inhibin B is markedly raised
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman whose periods stopped at 51 and who has had painless vaginal bleeding on and off for three months. She takes no hormone therapy and has never used tamoxifen.

She has hypertension treated with perindopril and a body mass index of 26 kg/m2. On examination her abdomen is soft with a palpable mass arising from the pelvis on the left. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 16 mm with a homogeneous appearance and a 7 cm predominantly solid left ovarian mass with moderate internal vascularity and no ascites. Pipelle biopsy of the endometrium reports simple hyperplasia without atypia. Her CA125 is 38 kU/L (less than 35), carcinoembryonic antigen is within normal limits, and inhibin B is markedly raised at several times the upper limit of the postmenopausal reference range.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with a firm mobile mass arising from the pelvis on the left, no ascites clinically, cervix looks normal with a small amount of fresh blood in the vault, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with endometrial thickness 16 mm of homogeneous appearance and a 7 cm predominantly solid left ovarian mass with moderate internal vascularity and no ascites, endometrial pipelle reporting simple hyperplasia without atypia, CA125 38 kU/L (less than 35), carcinoembryonic antigen within normal limits, inhibin B markedly raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Perform hysteroscopy and repeat endometrial sampling before deciding
options.rationale: Repeating endometrial assessment would only refine a diagnosis that has already been made and that is secondary to the ovarian lesion, and it does not alter the need for staging surgery. Hysteroscopy is valuable when sampling is inadequate or a focal cavity lesion is suspected on imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

options.text: Request colonoscopy and gastroscopy to find a primary bowel tumour
options.rationale: Endoscopy is directed at bilateral solid ovarian masses with a raised carcinoembryonic antigen where metastatic gastrointestinal disease is suspected, and here the mass is unilateral with a normal carcinoembryonic antigen. The oestrogenic effect on the endometrium also points to a hormonally active primary ovarian tumour. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system and rescan in six months
options.rationale: Progestogen treatment addresses hyperplasia without atypia when it is the whole problem, but here the hyperplasia is the downstream consequence of unopposed oestrogen from an ovarian lesion that will continue to drive it. Treating the endometrium while leaving the source in place also delays staging of a probable ovarian malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass

options.text: Arrange interval imaging of the ovarian mass in three months
options.rationale: Surveillance is appropriate for a simple unilocular cyst with reassuring features in a postmenopausal woman, not for a 7 cm solid vascular mass with a raised tumour marker and clinical evidence of oestrogen excess. Interval imaging here risks allowing a malignancy to progress. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass

options.text: Refer for gynaecological oncology review and surgical staging
options.rationale: A solid oestrogen secreting ovarian mass causing endometrial hyperplasia with a markedly raised inhibin B indicates a sex cord stromal tumour, and these are managed by laparotomy with hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical staging in a gynaecological oncology service. Inhibin is the marker that links the ovarian lesion to the endometrial finding and distinguishes this from an epithelial tumour, where CA125 typically rises far higher. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding demands endometrial assessment, but the finding of hyperplasia is a result rather than an endpoint and should always prompt the question of where the oestrogen is coming from. In a woman on no hormone therapy with a solid adnexal mass, the answer is often a hormonally active ovarian tumour, and adult granulosa cell tumours are the prototype: they account for a small share of ovarian malignancies, secrete oestrogen and inhibin, and commonly present with abnormal bleeding rather than the late abdominal distension typical of epithelial cancer. Inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone are the informative markers, since CA125 is often only marginally raised and can mislead a clinician into downgrading concern. Management is staging surgery in a specialist centre, and because these tumours can recur many years later, inhibin provides a long term surveillance marker after treatment.
key_points: Endometrial hyperplasia without exogenous hormones raises the question of an oestrogen source
A solid vascular postmenopausal adnexal mass requires oncology referral, not surveillance
Inhibin B is the marker of a sex cord stromal tumour; CA125 may be near normal
Bilateral solid masses with raised carcinoembryonic antigen suggest a gastrointestinal primary
Staging surgery includes hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
explanation.pearls: Adult granulosa cell tumours can recur decades after apparently curative surgery, so inhibin B is measured as a long term surveillance marker rather than only at diagnosis, and a rise in a woman who has been well for 15 years is a genuine signal rather than a laboratory artefact.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass
RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding
Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer optimal care pathway

subtopic_detail: Three mid pregnancy losses in a woman whose uterus shows a fundal indentation dividing the cavity with a normal external contour
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 30 year old woman referred after three pregnancy losses at 17, 19 and 16 weeks gestation, each preceded by painless cervical dilatation over a few hours with no bleeding beforehand. She has no living children.

She is well with a body mass index of 24 kg/m2 and takes no regular medication. Her antiphospholipid screen on two occasions twelve weeks apart is negative, her thyroid function and HbA1c are within normal limits, and parental karyotypes are normal. Three dimensional transvaginal ultrasound shows a smooth convex external fundal contour with an internal fundal indentation extending more than half the way down towards the internal os, dividing the cavity into two horns. Both ovaries appear normal and there are no fibroids. She asks what can be done before she tries again.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, single cervix and single vagina on speculum examination, uterus normal size and mobile bimanually
data_table.Investigations: Three dimensional transvaginal ultrasound with a smooth convex external fundal contour and an internal fundal indentation extending more than half way towards the internal os dividing the cavity, normal ovaries, no fibroids; lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart; thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits; HbA1c within normal limits; parental karyotypes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic division of the dividing tissue before conceiving
options.rationale: A normal external fundal contour with a deep internal indentation identifies a septate uterus rather than a bicornuate one, and hysteroscopic resection of the septum is a day procedure that is associated with improved live birth rates in women with recurrent mid trimester loss. Distinguishing it from a bicornuate uterus matters because the latter is not amenable to hysteroscopic treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage

options.text: Plan an elective cervical suture at twelve weeks in her next pregnancy
options.rationale: A history based suture is considered for recurrent loss attributed to cervical insufficiency once a structural uterine cause has been excluded or corrected, and placing one while a septum remains leaves the anatomical problem untreated. The painless dilatation history makes cervical surveillance part of the plan, but not before the cavity is addressed. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage

options.text: Start low dose aspirin with low molecular weight heparin when pregnant
options.rationale: That combination is the treatment for pregnancy loss associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, and her antibodies are negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, which is the sampling interval required to exclude it. Using it empirically exposes her to bleeding risk and injections for no established benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage

options.text: Refer for abdominal reconstruction to unify the two uterine horns
options.rationale: Open metroplasty is the operation for a genuine bicornuate uterus, which is identified by a deeply indented external fundal contour, and her external contour is smooth and convex. Performing laparotomy for a septate uterus subjects her to major surgery and a uterine scar when a hysteroscopic procedure would suffice. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage

options.text: Offer supportive early pregnancy care with serial scans and no intervention
options.rationale: Supportive care with reassurance scanning is the appropriate offer when investigation of recurrent loss finds no treatable cause, which is the outcome in roughly half of couples. Here a correctable structural abnormality has been identified, so declining to treat it is not a neutral choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage

explanation.summary: Congenital uterine anomalies are found in a minority of women investigated for recurrent pregnancy loss, and the septate uterus is the subtype most strongly associated with miscarriage and mid trimester loss because the poorly vascularised fibromuscular septum is a hostile implantation site. The critical diagnostic step is to distinguish a septate from a bicornuate uterus, and this rests on the external fundal contour: a septate uterus has a smooth or minimally indented external contour with a deep internal division, whereas a bicornuate uterus has an externally indented fundus reflecting failure of fusion rather than failure of resorption. Three dimensional ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging is needed because two dimensional imaging and hysterosalpingography show only the cavity and cannot see the external contour. Hysteroscopic septum resection is a low morbidity day procedure and is associated with improved live birth rates in this population, whereas a bicornuate uterus requires open metroplasty, an operation reserved for carefully selected cases.
key_points: The external fundal contour separates septate from bicornuate uterus
Two dimensional imaging shows only the cavity and cannot make that distinction
Septate uterus is the anomaly most associated with mid trimester loss
Hysteroscopic resection is a day procedure with improved live birth rates
Antiphospholipid antibodies must be negative on two samples twelve weeks apart
explanation.pearls: Hysterosalpingography and two dimensional ultrasound show an identical bifid cavity for septate and bicornuate uteri, so a woman who has already had either test still needs three dimensional ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging before any operation is planned.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage
European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology: Recurrent pregnancy loss guideline
BMJ Best Practice: Congenital uterine anomalies

subtopic_detail: A deepest pool of fifteen millimetres at thirty nine weeks with growth on the fiftieth centile, normal artery waveforms and no membrane rupture
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a day assessment unit seeing a 28 year old woman at 39 weeks and 2 days in her first pregnancy, referred because her midwife measured a symphysis fundal height 3 cm below expected. She reports normal foetal movements and denies any leaking of fluid.

Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal booking bloods and a normal glucose tolerance test. Her blood pressure has been consistently normal and her urine shows no protein. Ultrasound today reports an estimated foetal weight on the 50th centile with normal interval growth, a deepest amniotic fluid pool of 15 mm, a normal umbilical artery Doppler with positive end diastolic flow and a normal middle cerebral artery pulsatility index. A speculum examination shows no pooling of fluid and no visible fluid on coughing. Her cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 135 beats per minute with normal variability, two accelerations and no decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 135 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 3 cm below expected for gestation, cephalic presentation, speculum examination showing no pooling of amniotic fluid and no fluid seen on coughing, cervix closed and posterior
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound with estimated foetal weight on the 50th centile and normal interval growth, deepest amniotic fluid pool 15 mm, umbilical artery Doppler normal with positive end diastolic flow, middle cerebral artery pulsatility index normal, cardiotocograph with baseline 135 beats per minute, normal variability, two accelerations and no decelerations, urine dipstick showing no protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange twice weekly cardiotocography and rescan in one week
options.rationale: Surveillance without delivery is the strategy before term where prolonging the pregnancy still confers benefit, and at 39 weeks that benefit has largely gone while the risk associated with reduced liquor persists. Continuing to monitor exposes the foetus to that risk without gaining maturity. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth

options.text: Recommend induction of labour with continuous monitoring in labour
options.rationale: Isolated oligohydramnios at term with a normally grown foetus and normal Dopplers is an indication for birth, because at 39 weeks there is no maturity benefit from waiting while reduced liquor is associated with cord compression, meconium and intrapartum compromise. Induction rather than caesarean is appropriate given the reassuring growth and Dopplers, with continuous monitoring during labour to detect variable decelerations. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth

options.text: Advise maternal oral hydration and repeat the scan in 48 hours
options.rationale: Maternal hydration produces a small transient rise in measured liquor volume without changing perinatal outcome, so it manages the number rather than the pregnancy. Any short lived improvement would also risk falsely reassuring the team at a gestation where delivery is already appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth

options.text: Recommend caesarean section today because of the reduced liquor volume
options.rationale: Reduced liquor alone with normal growth, normal Dopplers and a normal cardiotocograph does not indicate abdominal delivery, and proceeding to caesarean forfeits the chance of a vaginal birth in a first pregnancy with consequences for all her future births. Caesarean becomes the answer if the cardiotocograph is abnormal or labour cannot be safely achieved. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth

options.text: Reassure her and return to routine midwifery care until 41 weeks
options.rationale: Routine care would be correct if the liquor volume were normal, since a small symphysis fundal height with normal growth on scan is otherwise reassuring. The deepest pool of 15 mm is a genuinely abnormal finding that changes the plan rather than an incidental one. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid volume is assessed either by the deepest vertical pool, with under 20 mm defining oligohydramnios, or by an amniotic fluid index under 50 mm, and Australian practice increasingly favours the single deepest pool because the index diagnoses more women without improving outcomes. Once oligohydramnios is confirmed the first task is to identify a cause, principally ruptured membranes, foetal growth restriction with placental insufficiency, a urinary tract anomaly in the foetus, or maternal drugs such as prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors and angiotensin blockade. Where none of these is present the diagnosis is isolated oligohydramnios, and the management question becomes one of timing of birth: before term the balance favours surveillance and steroid cover if early delivery becomes necessary, whereas at or near term the maturity argument for waiting disappears and birth is recommended. Continuous intrapartum monitoring matters because reduced liquor predisposes to cord compression and variable decelerations during labour.
key_points: A deepest vertical pool under 20 mm defines oligohydramnios
Exclude ruptured membranes, growth restriction, foetal renal anomaly and maternal drugs
Isolated oligohydramnios at term is an indication for birth
Normal growth and Dopplers support induction rather than caesarean
Reduced liquor predisposes to cord compression, so monitor continuously in labour
explanation.pearls: The amniotic fluid index identifies roughly twice as many women as having oligohydramnios compared with the single deepest pool, without any improvement in perinatal outcome but with more inductions and caesareans, which is why the deepest vertical pool is the preferred measure.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and timing of birth
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Amniotic fluid volume abnormalities
Cochrane Review: Amniotic fluid index versus single deepest vertical pocket

subtopic_detail: Solid masses on both ovaries with ascites in a woman whose gastric biopsy shows cells containing mucin that displaces the nucleus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 44 year old woman with four months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and a 6 kg weight loss. She has had intermittent epigastric discomfort for a year, attributed to reflux and treated with a proton pump inhibitor.

On examination her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and a firm mass palpable in each iliac fossa. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis shows bilateral solid ovarian masses measuring 9 cm on the right and 8 cm on the left, moderate ascites, and diffuse thickening of the gastric wall with enlarged perigastric nodes. Her CA125 is 210 kU/L (less than 35) and her carcinoembryonic antigen is raised. Gastroscopy performed yesterday shows a rigid infiltrated gastric body, and the biopsy is reported as a poorly cohesive adenocarcinoma whose cells contain abundant mucin displacing the nucleus to the periphery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with shifting dullness, firm mobile mass palpable in each iliac fossa, no hepatomegaly palpable, no palpable supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography showing bilateral solid ovarian masses 9 cm right and 8 cm left with moderate ascites, diffuse gastric wall thickening and enlarged perigastric nodes; CA125 210 kU/L (less than 35); carcinoembryonic antigen raised; gastroscopy showing a rigid infiltrated gastric body with biopsy reporting poorly cohesive adenocarcinoma with intracytoplasmic mucin displacing the nucleus; haemoglobin 98 g/L (115 to 155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange image guided biopsy of an ovarian mass before any treatment
options.rationale: The tissue diagnosis has already been obtained from the stomach and the ovarian histology would be expected to mirror it, so an additional biopsy adds delay and procedural risk. Biopsy of an adnexal mass would be justified if no primary had been identified and the histology remained unknown. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass

options.text: Perform therapeutic paracentesis and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: Draining ascites relieves symptoms and is a reasonable supportive measure alongside definitive management, but as the sole plan it leaves an aggressive malignancy untreated for a month. Symptom control belongs within the oncology pathway rather than instead of it. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer

options.text: Proceed to primary debulking surgery with total abdominal hysterectomy
options.rationale: Cytoreductive surgery is the treatment of a primary epithelial ovarian cancer, and operating on ovarian deposits that are metastases from a gastric primary offers no survival benefit while delaying systemic treatment. The histology of the gastric biopsy is what redirects the pathway away from ovarian cytoreduction. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer

options.text: Refer to the upper gastrointestinal multidisciplinary team for systemic therapy
options.rationale: Bilateral solid ovarian masses with a raised carcinoembryonic antigen and a gastric biopsy showing signet ring morphology indicate metastatic gastric cancer with ovarian deposits, so the disease is staged and treated as advanced gastric cancer by the upper gastrointestinal service with systemic therapy and biomarker testing. The ovarian masses are metastases and are not the primary target of treatment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer

options.text: Start carboplatin and paclitaxel for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer
options.rationale: That regimen is directed at epithelial ovarian cancer and is not the appropriate systemic therapy for a gastric adenocarcinoma, which is treated with fluoropyrimidine and platinum based combinations selected with reference to biomarkers. Choosing chemotherapy for the wrong primary is the consequence of anchoring on the ovarian masses. (Source: eviQ: Gastric cancer treatment protocols)
source_refs: eviQ: Gastric cancer treatment protocols

explanation.summary: Not every ovarian mass is a primary ovarian tumour, and metastatic disease accounts for a meaningful proportion of adnexal masses, with the stomach, colon, breast, appendix and pancreas the usual sources. The features that should prompt a search for a primary elsewhere are bilaterality, a solid rather than cystic architecture, relatively younger age, and a raised carcinoembryonic antigen with a CA125 that is elevated but not to the levels typical of advanced epithelial ovarian cancer. A Krukenberg tumour is specifically an ovarian metastasis containing mucin filled signet ring cells, most often from a diffuse type gastric carcinoma, and this histology is the single most useful piece of information because it settles the primary site and therefore the treatment pathway. Recognising the pattern spares the woman a laparotomy that would not help her and directs her instead to systemic therapy for advanced gastric cancer, where biomarker testing for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2, mismatch repair status and programmed death ligand 1 shapes drug selection.
key_points: Bilateral solid ovarian masses raise the possibility of metastatic disease
A raised carcinoembryonic antigen points away from a primary ovarian tumour
Signet ring cells with intracytoplasmic mucin define a Krukenberg metastasis
The gastric primary determines the treatment pathway, not the ovarian deposits
Cytoreductive ovarian surgery offers no survival benefit in this setting
explanation.pearls: Diffuse type gastric cancer can present with ovarian metastases while the stomach itself looks only mildly thickened, so a rigid poorly distensible stomach at gastroscopy in a woman with bilateral ovarian masses warrants biopsy even when the mucosa appears intact, because the tumour infiltrates the wall rather than forming an ulcer.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Optimal care pathway for people with stomach cancer
RANZCOG: Management of the adnexal mass
eviQ: Gastric cancer treatment protocols

subtopic_detail: No periods by sixteen with well developed breasts but almost no pubic or underarm hair, a short blind vagina and no uterus on scan
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16 year old who has never had a period. She is accompanied by her mother and has no pelvic pain of any kind, cyclical or otherwise.

She is 174 cm tall, which is above the centile predicted from her parents' heights. Breast development is Tanner stage 4 and she reports it began at about 11 years of age. Pubic and axillary hair are Tanner stage 1 with only a few fine hairs. External genitalia are female in appearance and examination reveals a short blind ending vagina about 4 cm deep with no visible cervix. Pelvic ultrasound and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging report absent uterus and absent upper vagina, with two soft tissue structures in the inguinal canals and no ovaries identified in the pelvis. Her serum testosterone is in the normal adult male range and her luteinising hormone is mildly raised.

data_table.Examination: Height 174 cm above the mid-parental predicted centile, breast development Tanner stage 4, pubic and axillary hair Tanner stage 1, normal female external genitalia, short blind ending vagina approximately 4 cm with no cervix visualised, soft non-tender swellings palpable in both inguinal canals, no acne or clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging reporting absent uterus and absent upper vagina with bilateral inguinal soft tissue structures and no pelvic ovaries, serum testosterone within the normal adult male range, luteinising hormone mildly raised, follicle stimulating hormone within the normal range, oestradiol at the lower end of the female range, renal tract normal on imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange surgical creation of a vaginal canal before she leaves school
options.rationale: First line management of vaginal length is graded self dilatation, which achieves satisfactory results in the majority and avoids operative morbidity, and it is undertaken when the young person is motivated rather than on a timetable set by others. Surgery is reserved for those in whom dilatation fails or is unacceptable. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence

options.text: Request renal tract imaging and spinal radiographs to complete her workup
options.rationale: Associated renal, skeletal and cardiac anomalies belong to Mullerian agenesis, where sexual hair development is normal because the ovaries and adrenals are intact and testosterone is in the female range. Her scanty sexual hair with male range testosterone points to a different diagnosis, and her renal tract is already reported as normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence

options.text: Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary service after karyotype confirmation
options.rationale: Normal breast development with almost absent sexual hair, a male range testosterone, an absent uterus and inguinal gonads indicate complete androgen insensitivity, and confirming the karyotype then referring to a specialist differences of sex development service is the appropriate step because decisions about gonadal management, timing of disclosure, psychological support and vaginal length all require coordinated expertise. Gonadectomy is not automatic and its timing is now individualised, which is precisely why the decision belongs to a multidisciplinary team with the young person involved. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic removal of both inguinal gonads on the next list
options.rationale: Proceeding directly to gonadectomy pre-empts a decision that depends on the specific diagnosis, the malignancy risk which is low before adulthood in this condition, and the young person's own participation once she understands her diagnosis. In complete androgen insensitivity the gonads also provide the oestrogen sustaining her breast development through aromatisation, so removal commits her to replacement therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence

options.text: Start cyclical oestrogen and progestogen to establish regular menstruation
options.rationale: There is no uterus, so no regimen can produce menstruation and prescribing one implies an outcome that cannot occur. Cyclical hormone therapy is the correct treatment for hypogonadism in a young woman who does have a uterus, such as in premature ovarian insufficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescence

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus but normal breast development narrows to two principal diagnoses, Mullerian agenesis and complete androgen insensitivity, and the discriminator is not the uterus but the sexual hair and the testosterone level. In Mullerian agenesis the ovaries and adrenals function normally, so pubic and axillary hair develop normally and testosterone sits in the female range, while renal, skeletal and cardiac anomalies are associated and must be sought. In complete androgen insensitivity a 46,XY individual has functioning testes producing male range testosterone, but absent androgen receptor function means no virilisation and no sexual hair, while aromatisation of that testosterone to oestrogen drives breast development; anti-Mullerian hormone from the testes regresses the Mullerian structures, which is why there is no uterus. Management is genuinely multidisciplinary, covering the timing and manner of disclosure to an adolescent, psychological support and peer contact, gonadal management informed by a malignancy risk that is low in childhood but rises in adulthood, oestrogen replacement if gonads are removed, bone health, and vaginal length managed first by graded dilatation.
key_points: Absent uterus with normal breasts narrows to Mullerian agenesis or androgen insensitivity
Sexual hair and testosterone level discriminate, not the absent uterus
Mullerian agenesis carries associated renal, skeletal and cardiac anomalies
In androgen insensitivity the gonads aromatise testosterone and sustain breast development
Graded vaginal dilatation precedes any consideration of surgery
explanation.pearls: Gonadectomy in complete androgen insensitivity has moved away from routine childhood removal, because germ cell malignancy risk is under about 2 per cent before adulthood and retaining the gonads preserves endogenous oestrogen, so the current approach is surveillance with the decision deferred until the young person can participate in it.
